shots.vo: The cable snaps. Your elevator drops from the *eightieth* floor.
You press against the wall. One idea from the movies: *jump* a second before impact. But will it work?
Floors flash by faster and faster. With no brakes, the basement is just *eight seconds* away, and you hit nearly *one hundred seventy* miles per hour.
A jump gives you maybe *six* miles per hour. It changes almost nothing.
Worse: inside a closed car, you can't see when the impact comes. Jump too early, and you'll *land on the floor* along with the elevator.
The MythBusters tested it: *busted*. Elevator experts say *lie flat on the floor*, so the impact spreads across your whole body.
And modern elevators have *safety brakes* that grab the guide rails on their own.
This really happened. On July twenty-eighth, nineteen forty-five, a bomber crashed into the Empire State Building.
Twenty-year-old elevator operator *Betty Lou Oliver* fell nearly *a thousand feet*, and survived.
Air trapped in the narrow shaft and the snapped cables, coiled below like a spring, saved her. It's still *a world record*.
